source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions (Memory & Cognition 24)
finding: A simplified CHREST (location-specific chunks only) was run on mirror-reflected positions, then humans were tested. Both showed the same cost of moving chunks to new places. This refutes Holding's claim that chunks are location-free.
numbers: Sim: 14 nets up to 70,000 nodes, 20 fixations (about 5 s). Recall normal 65.4% vs horizontal 63.2% (F(1,13)=19.80); vertical 53.3% and central 52.5%; gap to vertical/central 11.4%. Random positions in sim up to 23.4%. Human Exp 2: N=25 (5 Masters, 11 Experts, 9 Class A), 5 s views. Normal+horizontal 77.3/49.7/34.5% vs vertical+central 62.9/38.6/27.5% (Masters/Experts/Class A); contrast F(1,22)=96.79, skill x type F(2,22)=3.48, p<.05.
quote: Recall of modified positions should be greatly superior to recall of random positions.
limits: Small sample (25 players); chunk is operationalised by a 2 s inter-piece latency; the model has no templates here. Chase and Simon's omission-error pattern replicated only for Class A.
agent_relevance: A memory that keys stored units to exact context is needed; abstract-only keys lose recall in humans and in the model.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) same paper: random-position control and chunk counts
finding: Skill gap almost vanishes on random positions at 5 s. Chunks per position were few and small for random boards.
numbers: Chunks per position: game 4.0/4.3/2.5 and random 1.2/1.7/1.8 (Masters/Experts/Class A). Largest chunk in human positions: 10.1/7.1/6.1 pieces. Omission errors on random: 19.0/16.1/17.9. Chunks per recall (about 3.3-3.6) stayed within the 4-chunk visual STM limit.
limits: Chunk size depends on the latency rule and the apparatus (mouse added time). Commission errors on random: 2.4 (Masters), 5.5 (Experts), 3.9 (Class A).
agent_relevance: Working memory seen by the agent should hold about 3-4 pointers to big stored units, not many raw items.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of rapidly presented random chess positions is a function of skill (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 3)
finding: Review of 13 experiments (3-10 s views). Stronger players recalled more pieces on random boards in every study except Chase and Simon 1973, where one Master did worse than a novice. The old claim that expertise vanishes on random material is too strong.
numbers: 13 experiments; skill difference on random boards roughly one extra piece per 400 Elo points, far smaller than on game positions. Single small studies were usually not significant. F, t and p values were not reported consistently, so no pooled effect size.
limits: Narrative tally, not a weighted meta-analysis. The alternative that stronger players guess better was argued against with Jongman 1968 and commission errors.
agent_relevance: The expert edge on scrambled input is small but real: a larger chunk store finds accidental matches. Do not test a memory design on random input alone.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) Five seconds or sixty? Presentation time in expert memory (Cognitive Science 24)
finding: CHREST with templates predicted human recall from 1 s to 60 s for game and random positions. Recall follows a growth curve P=100-B*exp(-c(t-1)). Skill raises both the 1 s start and the rate of gain.
numbers: Humans: 20 players (5 Masters mean Elo 2498, 8 Experts 2121, 7 Class A 1879). Nets of 0.5K, 10K and 300K chunks for Class A, Expert, Master. Masters at 1 s match Experts at 10 s. Fit r2 for Experts and Class A averaged .69, Masters .35. Random positions: c doubles from Class A to Expert and triples to Master; game-to-random ratio of c about 6 (Experts, Class A) and nearly 25 (Masters). Parameters: STM 3 chunks; 50 ms to encode a chunk to STM, 250 ms into a template slot; about 8 s to add a new chunk; about 2 s to familiarise.
quote: Templates ... can store more pieces than the chunks hypothesized in Chase and Simon's model
limits: Only 5 Masters; Masters' fit is weaker (sim underestimates Masters at 5 s by 8%); net sizes are guesses, not measured; template slot threshold (3) is arbitrary.
agent_relevance: Gives concrete timing constants for a chunk memory: slow to learn new units, fast to read stored ones.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories (Cognition 66)
finding: Scores chunking, Holding's SEEK, long-term working memory (LT-WM, square and hierarchy versions) and template theory against about a dozen chess-memory findings. Template theory fits most; pure chunking fails on interference and multi-board recall.
numbers: Charness 1976: 30 s delay lowers recall only 6-8%. Multi-board: up to 4-5 boards recalled at about 60% correct; Cooke et al. used up to 9 boards. Masters place about 70% of 26 pieces after 1 s; Ellis 1973: 6.7 of 8 pieces (Class A) vs 4.5 (Class D) at 150 ms. Random positions: Masters about one third correct at 5 s and no more than two thirds at 60 s, which refutes the strong square-retrieval-structure version of LT-WM.
limits: Author built the template theory, so the scoring table is not neutral; several cited studies have 1-5 subjects.
agent_relevance: When comparing two memory designs, use discriminating tests (interference, many items, scrambled input), not recall of natural cases alone.

source: Gobet (1998) same paper: instruction and semantic orientation, single-subject work
finding: Level-of-processing results are used against chunking, but the paper argues chunking allows them if chunks give access to semantic memory. Lane and Robertson: a structural task hurts recall; the gap disappears if subjects know they must reconstruct.
numbers: Lane & Robertson 1979: judging/best-move task beats counting pieces at all skill levels; the difference vanished with advance warning. Goldin 1978: recognition above 70% for Class A even with a superficial task. Ericsson & Oliver single Expert: fast piece lookup (about 2 s) in a memorised game.
limits: Single-subject evidence (Ericsson & Oliver, Charness 1989 DH) needs replication; competing readings remain open.
agent_relevance: Instruction about later use changes encoding; tell the agent what the stored unit must support.

source: Gobet (1993) A computer model of chess memory (CogSci 15)
finding: First CHREST paper. It extends Simon and Gilmartin's MAPP with n-ary hierarchical nets, dynamic STM and links, then simulates random vs game, interference, multi-board and reflected positions.
numbers: Nets of 630, 2175 and 3646 nodes after 230, 1538 and 2843 positions; 20 fixations; STM set to 7. Model fits 97.4% of Class A results in one experiment and 77.5% in another. Random-position recall too high (7.7 pieces vs about 4 for humans).
limits: Early version: no templates, STM of 7, random-position recall overshoots humans, fixed internal representation across skill.
agent_relevance: Shows the revision cycle: model fails on random input, which then drove the template idea.

source: Gobet & Jackson (2001) In search of templates (ICCM)
finding: Two chess-naive adults trained over 15 sessions. Recall rose on a power curve and chunks grew; CHREST (no parameter tuning) matched the curves and predicted at most 3 chunks per recall.
numbers: Training fits: CE 39*N^.31 (r2=.93), JD 55*N^.23 (r2=.81). Above 90% correct near the end. Largest chunks near 10 pieces late. Model: 4,772 chunks and 107 templates (CE), 5,811 and 111 (JD). Correlation of fitted power-function parameters, model vs human: .99 for a and .93 for b. Templates explained about half of chunks of 4+ pieces in training and about 30% in test. Random positions: no significant power curve.
limits: N=2; model learned slower and made smaller chunks than humans; chunk-building rule (proximity) may differ from humans; templates mostly used via core, not slots (CE placed none in slots).
agent_relevance: Small-N test that a chunk store grows by exposure; the curve shape is the predictable signature.

source: Gobet & Jackson (2001), prior novice-training studies it cites
finding: Ericsson and Harris (1990) trained a novice to Master-like recall of game positions but not of random positions. Saariluoma and Laine (2001) trained two novices on 500 positions; CHREST fits their data as well as a frequency-based model and also fits the small random-position effect.
numbers: Saariluoma & Laine: game recall from about 15% to 40-50%, biggest gain in the first 100-150 positions; slight rise for random. Seen second-hand via Gobet & Jackson, not read directly.
limits: Second-hand report; small N in each study.
agent_relevance: Stored-unit growth shows fast early gains then diminishing returns.

source: Gong, Ericsson & Moxley (2015) Recall of briefly presented chess positions and its relation to chess skill (PLoS ONE)
finding: Near-replication of Chase and Simon's multi-trial recall with a new chunk-finding method (repeated recall) and a non-chess control group. Chess knowledge raises chunk count and size on game positions only; on random positions chunk measures did not track skill.
numbers: N=50 (25 rated players, class H to Expert; 25 non-players). Largest chunk, game positions: rated 4.56 (SD 1.67) vs non-players 2.60; random: rated 2.64 vs 2.08. Chunks: rated 2.74 game vs 1.30 random; non-players 1.02 vs 0.98. Among rated players only the largest chunk correlated with Elo; random-position chunk correlations with rating r(23) < .30, ns. Repeated-recall chunks predicted memory better than latency-defined chunks.
limits: Only 25 rated players, low rating range (no Masters), 1 s and 5 s views only. Authors say they lack power to find other mediators and doubt the reliability of latency chunks.
agent_relevance: Chunk size, not count, is the best single predictor: store large units. Latency-based chunk detection is noisy.

source: Gong et al. (2015) same: CHREST predictions tested
finding: Tests CHREST's predictions: smaller but present expertise gain on random boards; no skill difference in chunk number at brief views; more chess relations within than between chunks. Mixed support: the relation pattern held, but chunk number did not track rating.
numbers: Relations between consecutive pieces were negatively tied to latency, as in Chase and Simon. Number of chunks did not correlate with USCF rating in either position type.
limits: Procedure differs from Chase and Simon (computer, multi-trial); chunk definitions differ across the two techniques.
agent_relevance: Prefer measures that are stable across repeated trials when checking whether a stored unit is real.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields (Memory & Cognition 45)
finding: Across domains (games, music, programming, sports) experts keep a moderate advantage recalling random material. This is predicted by chunking and not by high-level schema or holistic-processing theories.
numbers: k=28 effects, 24 studies, N=903 (45 studies, 1,401 people in the sign test). Random-effects r=.41, 95% CI [.29,.51], I2=63%. After trim-and-fill for publication bias r=.29 [.17,.41]; fail-safe N=745. Sensitivity (2 flawed studies out): r=.39. Games r=.42 (k=11), music r=.69 (k=5), programming r=.36 (k=6), sports r=.30 (k=3, CI includes 0), other r=.24 (k=3, CI includes 0). Domain Q(4)=8.69, p=.069; exposure time not a moderator (Q(1)=0.89).
limits: Publication bias likely; domain and exposure time are confounded; music effect probably reflects less random stimuli; effects 40-50% bigger for structured material (r=.87 Knecht; .61 Gobet & Simon 2000). Could not test age or expertise level.
agent_relevance: Small-chunk coverage is a general expert mechanism, so a memory with many small reusable units helps even on novel input.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) background on randomisation method
finding: The random-position skill effect is not an artefact of one randomisation method; it holds when pieces are drawn with different probabilities (Gobet & Waters 2003, Waters & Gobet 2008), against Vicente and Wang (1998).
numbers: Chase and Simon's method reassigns the pieces of a game position to random squares. Chess Elo reliability r=.91 (Hambrick et al. 2014).
limits: Gobet & Waters and Vicente & Wang cited second-hand; not opened.
agent_relevance: Check that a test input is not easier or harder because of how it was randomised.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996b) multi-board and interference data as test of chunking vs templates (as reported in Gobet 1998)
finding: Large chunks (up to 15 pieces by the 2 s rule) in Masters let the original chunking model survive interference data, but inflate the chunk count needed in long-term memory. Templates (slots filled in under 1 s) avoid that inflation.
numbers: Up to 5 boards (5 s each) in Gobet & Simon 1996b; Frey & Adesman 1976: 2 boards at 8 s, 3 to 30 s of counting backwards, small loss.
limits: Estimates of chunk size depend on method; physical boards vs screens changed chunk size and number.
agent_relevance: Fixed-size items cannot explain results; items with fill-in slots can. Use slotted notes, not flat facts.

source: EPAM (Wikipedia): Feigenbaum & Simon 1962/1984, Richman et al. 1995 (EPAM IV)
finding: EPAM learns by growing a discrimination net. It began with nonsense-syllable learning (1962 serial position model) and was extended to expertise and concept formation. EPAM IV simulated expert memory.
numbers: Page gives dates only (late 1950s start; 1962, 1984, 1995, 1996, 1997 papers); no parameter values. The 8 s per new chunk comes from Gobet & Simon 2000.
limits: Encyclopaedia source; the primary EPAM IV paper was not read.
agent_relevance: Lineage EPAM to MAPP to CHREST; constants carry across versions.

source: CHREST (Wikipedia) and Gobet & Lane references
finding: CHREST is a symbolic chunk network with templates, eye-movement attention and an internal clock. It has also modelled children's vocabulary and syntax learning and concept formation. Noted limits: realistic-parameter constraint, weak on categorisation, rigid expert chunks (blind spots).
numbers: Visual STM = 3 chunks. The page gives no chess recall figures. Later work named: Lane & Chang (2018); Smith, Gobet & Lane (2007).
limits: Secondary source, no numbers; Lane and Chang 2018 not opened.
agent_relevance: A symbolic memory with a clock gives falsifiable timing predictions; our scaffold should log similar counts.

source: Chunking (psychology) (Wikipedia), incl. Franco & Destrebecqz 2012, Krivec et al. 2021
finding: Chunking explains expert recall in chess, and the gap shrinks on random positions. Counterpoints: Franco and Destrebecqz say the chunking model explains only parts of learning; the notion of chunk is loosely defined (Miller).
numbers: Chunk range 2-6 items; SF digit span 7 to about 80 with only 3-4 digits per chunk; PARSER holds up to 3 chunks.
limits: Secondary source; some inconsistency on whether chunks live in STM or LTM.
agent_relevance: Definition drift is a real risk: fix what counts as a chunk in our logs.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess
finding: Founding study. Master recalled game positions far better than a beginner but not random ones; 2 s pauses mark chunks; estimate of about 50,000 chunks for Masters. Not opened; facts as cited in Gobet & Simon 1996 and Gobet 1998.
numbers: Master did worse than a novice on random boards in this one study (few players), not replicated in later work.
limits: Very few subjects; later work finds a small skill effect on random boards.
agent_relevance: Origin of the chunk count that later work revises; do not treat 50,000 as measured.

source: Linhares & Freitas (2010) Questioning Chase and Simon's 'Perception in chess': the experience recognition hypothesis
finding: Rival account that questions Chase and Simon's chunk reading. Only title and DOI were seen via Crossref; content not read.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; method and sample unknown.
agent_relevance: Open rival to check before building on chunk counts.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in chess-playing language models (COLM)
finding: GPT models (25M and 50M parameters) trained on real PGN text keep a linear board-state code and estimate player skill. Starting from 20 random moves cuts win rate sharply, and a skill vector partly restores it.
numbers: Probe accuracy on board squares 99.6% (16 layer) and 99.1% (8 layer) vs 74.7% and 75.0% for randomised nets. Win rate vs Stockfish level 0 (5,000 games): standard board 69.6% (16L), 49.6% (8L); after 20 random moves 16.7% and 15.7%; with skill vector 43.2% and 31.3% (up to 2.6x). Elo probe called 99.4% of 4,000 random-start games low skill. Skill classification 90.5% (16L).
limits: Small models; character-level PGN; skill probe is below 1550 vs above 2050 only; Stockfish level 0 is a weak opponent. Not a direct test of chunk models.
agent_relevance: A game-trained model works well on typical positions and drops on scrambled ones, like humans on game vs random boards. This is not proof of chunks.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: 270M-parameter transformers trained on 10M Lichess games annotated by Stockfish reach grandmaster-level play without search on held-out boards, so recall of seen positions cannot explain it.
numbers: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 against humans; models of 9M, 136M and 270M; test set from 1K games of a different month (1.8M action values). Puzzle accuracy rises with data and model size. GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct included as baseline.
limits: Supervised on engine labels, not a chunk model; perfect distillation not reached; says nothing about learning speed or memory limits.
agent_relevance: Large pattern stores generalise to unseen positions: the strong form of chunk-like recognition at scale.

source: McGrath et al. (2022) Acquisition of chess knowledge in AlphaZero (PNAS)
finding: Probing AlphaZero for human chess concepts shows concepts appear in the network as training goes on, and opening play changes over training (comment from Kramnik). Abstract page only.
numbers: Abstract gives no figures.
limits: Abstract only; a game network, not a language model; probes show presence, not use.
agent_relevance: Learned systems build human-like units; useful when deciding which units to log in memory.

source: Jenner et al. (2024) Evidence of learned look-ahead in a chess-playing neural network
finding: Leela Chess Zero (a transformer) represents future best moves; attention heads move information across squares in time. Counter-view to a pure bag-of-heuristics reading.
numbers: A probe predicts the best move two turns ahead with 92% accuracy in positions with a single best line.
limits: Abstract page only; positions with one best line; one network.
agent_relevance: Pattern recognition and search are not exclusive; recognition can hold future-move cues.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) HiAgent: hierarchical working memory management with subgoals as memory chunks
finding: An LLM agent that stores a finished subgoal as one summarised chunk and drops the raw trace beats keeping all action-observation history. It cites Newell and Simon and Miller for the chunk idea; it is not a CHREST test.
numbers: Five AgentBoard long-horizon tasks. Success rate 21% to 42% overall, progress rate +23.94%, steps -3.8, context tokens -35%, run time -19.42%. Blocksworld SR 30 to 60, tyreworld 10 to 60, gripper 50 to 50, jericho 5 to 10. Ablation on tyreworld: no summarisation -30 points SR, no trajectory retrieval -10, neither -20. Subgoal-only (raw trace kept) still 20 points below HiAgent.
limits: Success rates move in steps of 5-10 points (few episodes per task); one model family; one significance test on steps; chunk is a prompt-level summary, with no learned discrimination net.
agent_relevance: Direct support for chunked working memory in an agent: keep the summary, retrieve detail on demand.

source: Gap check: LLM tests of CHREST/EPAM predictions
finding: No paper read in this pass runs a De Groot-style recall test (game vs scrambled position) on a language model, or tests CHREST/EPAM constants on one. Karvonen's random-opening test is the closest.
numbers: LLM studies found that test CHREST or EPAM directly: 0. Search tools (arXiv, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, web) were rate-limited or out of budget, so this is a coverage gap, not proof of absence.
limits: Coverage limited by rate limits.
agent_relevance: Open experiment: give our agent game vs scrambled boards and fit the growth curve P=100-B*exp(-c(t-1)).

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) discussion: where the template model misses humans
finding: Model misses: it underestimates Master recall; the human bulge in chunk number (up then down) is only partly reproduced; early physical-board studies inflated chunk number and cut chunk size.
numbers: Human Masters' chunk count: 2.9 at 1 s, 4.2 at 4 s, 3.3 at 10 s. Experts' largest chunks: about 9-10 at 1 s rising to about 17 at 60 s; Class A about 4-5. New node about 8 s, familiarise about 2 s, elaborate a template minutes or longer.
limits: Authors suggest bigger nets or more templates would fix Masters' fit; not tested.
agent_relevance: Time-to-learn constants (seconds) justify caching verified results instead of re-deriving them.

source: Gobet & Simon (2000) random-position result as a test between rival theories
finding: Random-position skill effect separates theories: high-level schema or holistic accounts predict none, chunk and template accounts predict a small one, square-level retrieval structures predict a large one. Data: small effect.
numbers: Random positions: skill levels differ at 10 s or less, F(2,15)=7.74, p<.005, and at longer times F(2,16)=14.36, p<.001. Masters recall about 17 of 26 pieces (68%) after 60 s (Gobet 1998).
limits: Significance rests on 5 Masters, 8 Experts, 7 Class A; effect small in absolute terms.
agent_relevance: Choose tests on which rival designs predict differently.
